name: The Poverty of the Stimulus
statement: Children learn a grammar richer than anything their limited, uncorrected input could have taught them.
statementAccent: richer than anything their limited, uncorrected input could have taught them
meaning: The poverty of the stimulus is an argument central to Chomskyan linguistics that the linguistic knowledge children acquire is underdetermined by the input they receive. The speech a child hears is finite, noisy with errors and false starts, and lacking systematic negative evidence, correction of what is ungrammatical, yet children reliably and rapidly converge on a rich, abstract, systematic grammar that goes far beyond that input. From this gap the argument concludes that some grammatical knowledge must be innate, supplying the constraints the data cannot. It is the chief motivation for universal grammar, and one of the most disputed claims in the study of language.
mechanism: The argument is a learnability inference: given only the positive evidence a child actually encounters, no general learner could reliably arrive at the specific abstract grammar attained, so language-specific innate knowledge must bridge the gap. Its classic illustration is the structure-dependence of grammatical rules. To turn a statement into a yes-no question, English speakers move the structurally main auxiliary, never simply the first auxiliary in the string, yet children are said rarely to hear the complex sentences that would rule out the simpler, wrong rule. Add the absence of systematic correction, children are not reliably told which sentences are ungrammatical, and the input looks too impoverished to explain the outcome.

examples.text: Children forming questions use a rule sensitive to hierarchical structure rather than linear word order, and never make the tempting first-auxiliary error, even though the disambiguating sentences are claimed to be rare.
Children receive mostly positive evidence, hearing what is said but not being systematically corrected for ungrammatical errors, yet they converge on a grammar that excludes them.
The argument is a species of Plato's problem, how humans come to know so much from so little experience, applied to grammar.

variants.name: The learnability argument
variants.text: The formal version framing the question as what a learner could in principle induce from a given input, and arguing that the target grammar is not so inducible without innate bias.

variants.name: Domain-general responses
variants.text: The counter-position that any needed innate bias may be general-purpose, so structure can be learned from realistic input without a dedicated language faculty.

whyItMatters: The poverty of the stimulus is the linchpin argument for linguistic nativism and universal grammar, shaping decades of debate in linguistics, cognitive science, and philosophy about how much of the mind is built in. It sharpened questions about what children actually hear, what counts as learning, and whether general cognition or language-specific endowment does the work, and it drove the development of statistical and Bayesian models of acquisition designed to test it. Whether or not it succeeds, it forced the field to make its assumptions about input and learning explicit and testable.

working.text: ask whether the grammar a child attains could plausibly be induced from the specific evidence the child actually received.
note the claimed scarcity of disambiguating sentences and the absence of systematic correction, the two planks of the argument.
treat the impoverished-input claim as an empirical hypothesis to be checked against corpora, not an established fact.

limits: The argument is heavily contested, and its empirical premise is exactly what critics dispute. Pullum and Scholz argued in 2002 that the crucial input, such as the relevant complex questions, is actually attested in corpora, so the claim of impoverished data is unsupported. Statistical and Bayesian learning models, notably by Perfors, Tenenbaum, and Regier, show that an ideal learner with general-purpose, not language-specific, capacities can prefer the hierarchical grammar from realistic input, learning structure-dependence without innate universal grammar. Nativists such as Berwick and Chomsky have replied that these results smuggle in structural assumptions, so the matter remains unresolved.
misreadings: The argument does not claim language is entirely innate; it holds that some specific grammatical knowledge is innate, with input still essential. It is not a claim that children hear very little speech overall, but that they lack the particular disambiguating data and the negative evidence needed to fix certain abstract rules. No negative evidence does not mean no feedback of any kind, only the absence of systematic correction of grammatical errors. And it is an argument, not a single empirical finding, whose force depends on premises about the input that are themselves contestable.
origin: The term was coined by Noam Chomsky in 'Rules and Representations' (1980), though the underlying argument appears earlier, in his 1965 'Aspects of the Theory of Syntax'; it was critically assessed by Pullum and Scholz in 2002.

sources.text: Poverty of the stimulus, Wikipedia. — the underdetermination argument, structure-dependence, the no-negative-evidence point, and the criticisms.
Pullum & Scholz, 'Empirical assessment of stimulus poverty arguments,' The Linguistic Review 19:9-50 (2002). — the challenge that the crucial input is attested in corpora.
